references.excerpt: SIESTA, AnSTROKE, GOLIATH showed no deleterious effects of general anesthesia on patient outcome after EVT compared with conscious sedation. Two of the possible mechanisms of this finding are systolic hypotension and hypocapnia.

references.excerpt: 5 RCTs with 498 patients were included. GA was conducted in 251 patients and CS in 247 patients. EVT under GA in AIS patients had higher rates of successful recanalization (RR: 1.13, 95% CI: 1.04-1.23; P = 0.004) and functional independence at 3 months (RR: 1.28, 95% CI: 1.05-1.55; P = 0.013) than CS. However, GA was associated with higher risk of mean arterial pressure (MAP) drop (RR: 1.71, 95% CI: 1.19-2.47) and pneumonia (RR: 2.32, 95% CI: 1.23-4.37). There was no difference between GA and CS groups in mortality at 3 months.

cards.question: What are the AAGBI recommendations for anaesthesia in remote locations?
cards.answer: Same standards as theatre: trained anaesthetic assistant, full monitoring including capnography, anaesthetic machine checked, reliable suction and oxygen, emergency drugs and difficult-airway equipment immediately available, two-way communication with the main theatre suite, and a clear plan for transfer if deterioration occurs.

cards.question: How is contrast-induced nephropathy prevented in IR patients?
cards.answer: Distinguish CA-AKI (association) from CI-AKI (causation). Assess AKI, stable CKD, route, urgency and fluid tolerance. ESUR uses <45 for first-pass arterial exposure/ICU and <30 for IV/second-pass exposure. Individualise saline in high-risk patients; no NAC or prophylactic dialysis. Medication decisions are not blanket holds. Do not delay essential emergency imaging. See the detailed ICU AKI & RRT contrast lesson.

cards.question: What are the anaesthetic considerations for endovascular thrombectomy in acute stroke?
cards.answer: Both techniques are acceptable. The three randomised trials (SIESTA, ANSTROKE and GOLIATH) found no harm from general anaesthesia compared with conscious sedation, and a pooled analysis of five trials found general anaesthesia associated with higher recanalisation and 3-month functional independence — but more intra-procedural hypotension and pneumonia, with no mortality difference. The strongest determinant of outcome is haemodynamic management rather than the technique: avoid MAP below 70 mmHg and hypocapnia, maintain normoglycaemia and normothermia, and never delay reperfusion for an anaesthetic decision. Speed is critical — door-to-puncture <90 min; immediate post-procedure neuro-imaging is required.
